nameStory: This microscopic green alga doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its scientific name, Xanthidium wewahitchkense. The genus name 'Xanthidium' comes from the Greek word 'xanthos' meaning yellow, referring to the golden-green color these tiny organisms can display under certain conditions.
description: Xanthidium wewahitchkense is a single-celled freshwater alga that's invisible to the naked eye, measuring only about 30-50 micrometers across (smaller than the width of a human hair). This microscopic organism has a distinctive star-like or spiky appearance when viewed under a microscope, with ornate projections extending from its cell wall. It belongs to a group called desmids, which are among the most beautiful and geometrically perfect organisms in the microscopic world. You'll need at least a 400x magnification microscope to see its intricate details.

idTips.label: Cell shape
idTips.description: The cell appears roughly circular to oval with symmetrical spiny projections radiating outward, creating a star-burst or medieval mace-like appearance under the microscope

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Measures 30-50 micrometers in diameter, requiring high magnification to observe clearly - about the size of a small dust particle

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Appears bright green to golden-green under normal lighting, with chloroplasts (green structures) visible as darker patches within the cell

idTips.label: Surface texture
idTips.description: Cell wall shows intricate patterns of pores, bumps, and ridges that create a highly ornate, jewel-like appearance under high magnification

idTips.label: Movement
idTips.description: Typically stationary or very slowly rotating in place, unlike swimming algae - it may appear to gently rock or drift with water currents

habitat: Found in clean, slightly acidic freshwater environments throughout New England, particularly in bog ponds, pristine lakes, and slow-moving streams with low nutrient levels. Look for it in the shallow, sunlit areas of these water bodies where it can photosynthesize effectively. It prefers cool, unpolluted waters and is often considered an indicator of good water quality.

seasonality.spring: Most active period as water temperatures rise and daylight increases, making this the best time to find specimens in water samples from clean ponds and streams.
seasonality.summer: Continues to be present but may be less abundant during hot periods when water temperatures peak and oxygen levels drop in shallow waters.
seasonality.fall: Still observable as temperatures cool, often forming small populations in protected coves and bog margins before winter dormancy.
seasonality.winter: Present but largely dormant under ice cover, though specimens can still be found in samples from ice-free flowing water or greenhouse cultures.

funFact: Despite being invisible to the naked eye, this tiny alga creates some of the most geometrically perfect and intricate patterns in nature - its cell wall decorations are so precise and beautiful that Victorian microscopists collected and arranged them into stunning kaleidoscopic art pieces that sold for hundreds of dollars.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other spiny desmids in the same genus, but the specific arrangement and shape of its projections create a unique 'fingerprint' pattern. A helpful memory trick: imagine a medieval morning star weapon shrunk down to microscopic size - that spiky, symmetrical appearance is characteristic of this species.
contextualKnowledge: The species name 'wewahitchkense' likely refers to the location where it was first scientifically described, following the botanical tradition of naming species after their discovery location. Many desmids like this one are used as indicator species by environmental scientists because they're very sensitive to pollution and only thrive in clean water.
compareHints: Compared to its relatives like Xanthidium cristatum or X. armatum, this species has a more rounded overall outline with shorter, less elaborate spines. While X. cristatum has pronounced crest-like projections and X. armatum features longer, more weapon-like spines, X. wewahitchkense maintains a more compact, star-burst appearance with moderate-length projections that are evenly distributed around the cell.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Xanthidium relatives, antilopaeum has the most modest spination - while species like armatum and cristatum sport dramatic long spines, antilopaeum's decorations are more like small bumps and short projections.
